content.title: About
content.content: Plain wheat crackers, known as Wheat Thins, are thin, crunchy biscuits made from whole wheat. They have a light salty flavor, a subtle whole‑grain aroma, and a crisp texture. The snack is often enjoyed on its own or paired with cheese, dips, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat Thins were first introduced in the United States in 1947 and have become a classic snack.
Whole‑wheat crackers contain more dietary fiber than typical white crackers.
They are frequently used in recipes as a base for mini‑pizzas or bite‑size appetizers.
The original recipe uses a small amount of vegetable oil and salt, with no added sugar.
Packaging usually holds 200 g, enough for several servings.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole wheat provides fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Unlike many sweet snacks, these crackers contain virtually no sugar, helping blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat supplies thiamine, niacin, and folate, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from whole grain helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The snack has a modest amount of fat, mainly from plant sources.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy should avoid them.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although moderate, those limiting salt should account for the sodium.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Crackers can raise blood sugar quickly, so consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy them as a standalone snack, with cheese, hummus, guacamole, or use them in recipes—such as a base for mini‑pizzas, pâté bites, or as crunchy topping for salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in the original package or an airtight container. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to prevent oil oxidation.

meat-loaf-made-with-chicken-or-turkey.title: Meat loaf made with chicken or turkey

content.title: About
content.content: Meat loaf made with chicken or turkey is a baked dish prepared from ground white poultry meat, eggs, breadcrumbs, and seasonings. It has a tender texture, mild flavor, and is often used as a lower‑fat alternative to traditional beef meat loaf.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey meat loaves contain less saturated fat than their beef counterpart.
The use of white meat makes the loaf high in protein and gives it a lighter color.
Typical recipes add onion, garlic, and herbs such as thyme or rosemary for extra aroma.
Poultry meat loaf is frequently served cold, sliced for sandwiches.
When baked correctly, the interior stays moist while the crust turns golden.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, poultry meat loaf has fewer saturated fats, supporting heart health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The loaf offers iron, zinc, and phosphorus, nutrients needed for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Relatively low in calories
items.content: With moderate amounts of breadcrumbs and fat, the dish remains relatively light in calories.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Risk of salmonella
items.content: Undercooked poultry can harbor harmful bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If broth or sauces are added, the sodium level can become high.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Prepared mixes may contain preservatives or flavor enhancers that some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the meat loaf thinly for sandwiches, serve with vegetable salads, roasted potatoes or rice. It also works well cubed in salads or soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked loaf in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C) before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy yogurt is a fermented beverage made from soy milk. It has a creamy texture, a mildly tangy flavor, and is often fortified with vitamins and minerals to match the nutritional profile of traditional dairy yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soy yogurt is suitable for vegans and people with lactose intolerance.
It is frequently fortified with calcium and vitamin D to compensate for the lower natural levels in soy milk.
Soy products contain isoflavones, which may have beneficial effects on hormonal balance.
Unlike dairy yogurt, soy yogurt typically contains no cholesterol.
Manufacturers often add probiotic strains such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium to support gut health.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of soy yogurt provides about 6–8 g of protein, useful for maintaining muscle mass.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Fortified soy yogurt can deliver up to 30 % of the daily calcium requirement, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in sugar (when unsweetened)
items.content: Plain soy yogurt contains little sugar, making it suitable for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Contains isoflavones
items.content: Soy isoflavones may support heart health and act as antioxidants.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Probiotics in the yogurt help balance intestinal flora and improve digestive function.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis when consuming soy yogurt.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Soy contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals if consumed in excess.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Some brands sweeten their soy yogurt, increasing calorie content and glycemic impact.

items.title: GMO concerns
items.content: Much of the commercial soy supply is genetically modified; choose non‑GMO labeled products if this matters to you.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soy yogurt can be enjoyed on its own, blended into smoothies, mixed with granola, fruit salads, or used as a base for sauces and desserts. Sweeten with honey, maple syrup, or fresh berries if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store soy yogurt in the refrigerator at 2–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days and do not leave it at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
